comprehensionMCQs.question: Three co-accused 'A', 'B', and 'C' are convicted of dacoity with murder and sentenced to death. The President commutes the death sentence of 'A' to life imprisonment. The mercy petition of 'B' is rejected without any distinguishing factors on the identical record. 'B' approaches the Supreme Court under Article 32 on the eve of execution. How will the Court decide applying the rule in Harbans Singh v. State of U.P. (1982)?
options: Execution must proceed because the President has absolute discretion
Stay the execution and commute 'B''s death sentence to life imprisonment to maintain parity under Article 14 and prevent an irreversible miscarriage of justice
Order 'A' to be executed as well
Direct the President to reconsider all three cases in open court
comprehensionMCQs.explanation: In Harbans Singh (1982), the Supreme Court held that where identically situated co-accused have their sentences commuted, executing the remaining co-accused violates Article 14 and justice, requiring parity in clemency.

comprehensionMCQs.question: Following a general election, a new Central Government assumes power in New Delhi. While the President need not assign reasons in the removal order, the power cannot be exercised arbitrarily, capriciously, or for political reasons; removal solely because the Governor does not share the political ideology of the new ruling party is unconstitutional
Governors cannot be removed before completing 5 years under any circumstances
The State Legislature must ratify the removal
comprehensionMCQs.explanation: The 5-Judge Bench in B.P. Singhal (2010) held that the "pleasure of the President" does not authorize arbitrary dismissal. Removing a Governor merely because of a change of government at the Centre is an unconstitutional exercise of power.

title: Case Study 200: Union & State Executive, Clemency & Remission (Articles 52–78, 153–167) (Article 53 — Original Civil Suit / Declaratory Relief)

2. DOCTRINAL & STATUTORY ANALYSIS (Union & State Executive, Clemency & Remission (Articles 52–78, 153–167)): Core constitutional framework under Union & State Executive, Clemency & Remission (Articles 52–78, 153–167). Applying the core concept of 'Pocket Veto', the impugned disciplinary dismissal / disqualification order by the Municipal Corporation / Panchayat Authority must satisfy legality, rational nexus, and proportionality. As reinforced by In State of Haryana v. Jagdish (2010), the Supreme Court settled that the remission policy prevailing on the date of conviction governs. A subsequent harsher policy cannot be applied retrospectively to defeat a life convict's consideration.

3. comprehensionMCQs.question: A convict was convicted of gang rape and murder in 1995 when the State's 1992 Remission Policy was in force, which permitted life convicts to be considered for premature release after 14 years. In 2014, the State framed a new policy completely barring remission for convicts convicted of rape and murder. In 2022, the convict applies for premature release. The State rejects his application relying on the harsher 2014 policy. The convict challenges this under Article 226. What will the High Court decide?
options: The 2014 policy applies because it was in force when the application was heard

The application must be considered under the 1992 policy that was in force on the date of his conviction (State of Haryana v. Jagdish 2010); a subsequent harsher policy cannot be applied retrospectively to deny consideration for remission
The convict must be released immediately without any evaluation
The policy of the neighboring state applies
comprehensionMCQs.explanation: In State of Haryana v. Jagdish (2010), the Supreme Court settled that the remission policy prevailing on the date of conviction governs. A subsequent harsher policy cannot be applied retrospectively to defeat a life convict's consideration.

comprehensionMCQs.question: The Governor of a State refuses to take any action on Bills passed by the State Legislative Assembly, claiming that because the Speaker had adjourned the Assembly sine die instead of the Governor proroguing it under Article 174, all sittings and legislative enactments passed during the reconvened session were illegal and non-existent in law. What was the Supreme Court's decisive finding on this executive claim in State of Punjab (2023)?
options: The Governor's stand was constitutionally sound

The Governor's stand was completely unlawful: the Speaker has exclusive authority under Assembly Rules to adjourn the House sine die and reconvene it; the session was lawful and continuous, and an unelected Governor has zero constitutional power to invalidate sittings of an elected assembly or stall legislation
The Assembly stood automatically dissolved
The Chief Minister was liable to be dismissed
comprehensionMCQs.explanation: In State of Punjab (Nov 2023), the 3-Judge Bench held that the Governor cannot declare a legislative session invalid or use procedural disagreements with the Speaker as a pretext to sit on bills passed by elected lawmakers.
